title: Hand-Arm Vibration
osha_standards: OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) General Duty Clause
summary: Vibration from power tools, machinery, and heavy equipment can damage the blood supply and nerves in your fingers and toes. Use low-vibration tools, take breaks, and report symptoms like tingling or white fingertips.
talking_points: Vibration from power tools, machinery, vehicles, and heavy equipment affects the blood supply to the fingers and toes. It can be serious and disabling.

Warning signs include tingling in the hand and fingertips that turn white and lose feeling. In one story, a carpenter with these signs was diagnosed with Raynaud's syndrome from vibrating tools. It can lead to tissue damage and may require surgery.
Wear gloves or anti-vibration wraps to improve grip and lessen the shock of vibrating tools.
Take regular breaks when you use tools that cause vibration.
Ask your employer to buy tools, bits, sawblades, and grinding wheels designed for reduced vibration, and power tools with handles isolated from the vibrating part.
Keep tools maintained. Ask your employer to have them serviced regularly.
Heavy equipment operators can ask for seat padding and dampening materials on the engine and cab floor.
Use cutting or power head dampening devices where they are available.
site_hazards_to_check: Jackhammers, grinders, chipping tools, and saws with worn parts or no anti-vibration features
Workers using vibrating tools for long stretches with no breaks
Tools with dull bits, blades, or wheels that are not maintained
Heavy equipment with worn seat padding or no dampening on the cab floor
Workers reporting tingling, numbness, or white fingertips
discussion_questions: Which tools on this job vibrate the most, and how are we limiting time on them?
What symptoms should make you tell your supervisor or see a doctor?
What low-vibration tools, handles, or wraps could we ask for?

flags: Verified against CPWR Vibration: Hand and Arm toolbox talk: blood supply/serious and disabling, Kevin's Raynaud's story (white fingertips, tissue damage, surgery), gloves or anti-vibration wraps, regular breaks, reduced-vibration tools/bits/blades/wheels, isolated handles, maintenance, seat padding and cab/engine dampening, power head dampening. Nothing invented; 8 points; no UK wording.

Citation OSH Act Section 5(a)(1) is the only standard the source prints; it is a statute rather than a 1926 section. No specific OSHA 1926 standard governs hand-arm vibration, so this is acceptable. Talk does not cite an exposure limit (none exists in OSHA), correctly.
